{{nowrap|[[List of Formula One World Constructors' Champions|Constructors' Champion]]: [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]]}} }} [[File:Anefo 932-2378 Keke Rosberg, Zandvoort, 03-07-1982 - Restoration.jpg|thumb|upright|Keke Rosberg won his first and only [[List of Formula One World Drivers' Champions|Drivers' Championship]] with [[Williams Grand Prix Engineering|Williams]] with 44 points, despite having trailed for most of the season and having only won one race.|alt=Black-and-white photograph of Keke Rosberg]] [[File:Didier Pironi (Zandvoort 1982).jpg|thumb|[[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]] won the [[List of Formula One World Constructors' Champions|Constructors' Championship]] with the [[Ferrari 126C|126C2]].|alt=Red Ferrari racing car exiting a corner during a race]] The '''1982 FIA Formula One World Championship''' was the 36th season of [[Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile|FIA]] [[Formula One]] motor racing. It included two competitions run over the course of the year, the 33rd [[List of Formula One World Constructors' Champions|Formula One World Championship for Drivers]] and the 25th [[List of Formula One World Constructors' Champions|Formula One World Championship for Constructors]]. The season featured sixteen rounds between 23 January and 25 September. The Drivers' Championship was won by [[Keke Rosberg]] and the Constructors' Championship by [[Scuderia Ferrari]]. The Championship started with a drivers' strike at [[1982 South African Grand Prix|the season opener in South Africa]] and saw a partial race boycott as part of the ongoing [[FISA–FOCA war]] at the [[1982 San Marino Grand Prix|San Marino Grand Prix]]. Two drivers died during 1982: [[Gilles Villeneuve]] during qualifying for the [[1982 Belgian Grand Prix|Belgian Grand Prix]] and [[Riccardo Paletti]] at the start of the [[1982 Canadian Grand Prix|Canadian Grand Prix]]. Championship front-runner [[Didier Pironi]] also suffered a career-ending accident while qualifying for the [[1982 German Grand Prix|German Grand Prix]]. These incidents and several other major accidents led to regulation changes to increase driver safety for [[1983 Formula One World Championship|the 1983 season]]. Motorsport journalist [[Nigel Roebuck]] later wrote that 1982 was "an ugly year, pock-marked by tragedy, by dissension, by greed, and yet, paradoxically, it produced some of the most memorable racing ever seen".{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=170}} Eventual champion Rosberg won only one race all season – the [[1982 Swiss Grand Prix|Swiss Grand Prix]] – but consistency gave him the Drivers' Championship, five points clear of Pironi and [[John Watson (racing driver)|John Watson]]. Rosberg was the second driver to win the championship having won only one race in the season, after [[Mike Hawthorn]] in {{F1|1958}}. Eleven different drivers from seven different teams won a race during the season, with no driver winning more than twice; there was also a run of nine different winners in nine consecutive races from the [[1982 Monaco Grand Prix|Monaco Grand Prix]] to the Swiss Grand Prix. Ferrari, who replaced Villeneuve with [[Patrick Tambay]] and Pironi with {{F1|1978}} World Champion [[Mario Andretti]], managed to score enough points to secure the Constructors' Championship, finishing five points clear of [[McLaren]] with [[Renault in Formula One|Renault]] third. Rosberg's team Williams finished fourth in the Constructors' standing a further four points behind McLaren, marking the only time since the Constructors' Championship was introduced in 1958 that a team containing the eventual Drivers' Champion finished outside the top 3 of the Constructors' standings. == Drivers and constructors == The following teams and drivers took part in the 1982 Formula One World Championship: {| |- valign="top" | {| class="wikitable sortable" style="font-size: 85%" |- valign="top" |+ List of entrants into the 1982 Formula One World Championship |- ! scope="col" |Entrant ! scope="col" |Constructor ! scope="col" |Chassis ! scope="col" |Engine ! scope="col" |Tyres ! scope="col" |{{Tooltip|No.|Number}} ! scope="col" |Driver ! scope="col" |{{Tooltip|Rounds|Rounds entered}} |- | scope="row" rowspan="4"| {{flagicon|GBR}} [[Parmalat]] [[Brabham|Racing]] !rowspan="2"| [[Brabham]]-[[BMW in Formula One|BMW]] |rowspan="2"| [[Brabham BT50|BT50]] |rowspan="2"| [[BMW M12]]/13 1.5 [[Inline-four engine|L4t]] |rowspan="4"| {{Goodyear}} | 1 | {{flagicon|BRA|1968}} [[Nelson Piquet]] | 1, 5–16 |- | 2 | {{flagicon|ITA}} [[Riccardo Patrese]] | 1, 5, 9–16 |- !rowspan="2"| [[Brabham]]-[[Ford Motor Company|Ford]] |rowspan="2"| [[Brabham BT49C|BT49C]]

October 2020}} == Background == === Politics === [[File:Ecclestone 1991 cropped.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Bernie Ecclestone]] ''(pictured in 1991)'', owner of [[Brabham]] and chairman of [[Formula One Constructors Association|FOCA]], was one of the leading figures in the [[FISA–FOCA war]].|alt=Portrait of Bernie Ecclestone]] Starting in the early 1970s, [[Bernie Ecclestone]], owner of the Brabham team, had seized control of the Formula 1 Constructors Association, later renamed Formula One Constructors' Association. In this role, he began to negotiate more lucrative contracts between the teams and the track owners, including obtaining full control over television rights for FOCA.{{cite web|last1=Diepraam|first1=Mattijs|title=Poachers turned gamekeepers: how the FOCA became the new FIA|url=http://8w.forix.com/fiasco-introduction-timeline.html|website=forix.com|publisher=Haymarket Media Group|access-date=28 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180128182350/http://8w.forix.com/fiasco-introduction-timeline.html|archive-date=28 January 2018|date=21 November 2007}} Realising the growing influence of Ecclestone and FOCA, the sport's governing body, the [[Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile]] (FIA) and its head, [[Paul Alfons von Metternich-Winneburg|Paul Metternich]], instated Frenchman [[Jean-Marie Balestre]] as the head of the Commission Sportive Internationale in 1978, which was then renamed to [[Fédération Internationale du Sport Automobile]] (FISA). FIA delegated running of the sporting regulations governing Formula One to FISA.{{cite web|last1=Saward|first1=Joe|title=Why has FISA been abolished?|url=http://www.grandprix.com/ft/ft00162.html|website=grandprix.com|access-date=28 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180128183205/http://www.grandprix.com/ft/ft00162.html|archive-date=28 January 2018|date=1 September 1993}} Over the following years, a power struggle developed between FOCA and FISA and Ecclestone and Balestre in particular. This conflict is generally referred to as the [[FISA–FOCA war]].{{cite web|title=FISA/FOCA war|url=https://www.autosport.com/f1/news/27685/fisafoca-war|website=autosport.com|access-date=28 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180128185406/https://www.autosport.com/f1/news/27685/fisafoca-war|archive-date=28 January 2018|date=1 June 1980}} FOCA consisted of the majorly British constructor teams, while the [[Factory-backed|manufacturer or "works" teams]] (Renault, Ferrari, [[Alfa Romeo in Formula One|Alfa Romeo]] and [[Equipe Ligier|Talbot-Ligier]]), together with Osella and Toleman were aligned with FISA.{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=10 & 92}}{{efn|Lang gives the FISA teams in 1980 as "Ferrari, Renault, Alfa-Romeo, Talbot-Ligier and Osella". By April 1982, Toleman has been added to the list, but "Guy Ligier had recently switched allegiance to FOCA".{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=10 & 92}}}} The conflict came to a head at the [[1980 Spanish Grand Prix]], where the drivers of teams belonging to FOCA boycotted the obligatory drivers' briefing and were threatened by FISA with having their licences revoked. The race went ahead as a non-championship event, without the non-FOCA aligned teams participating. Following an aborted attempt to establish a breakaway World Championship, FOCA agreed to the [[Concorde Agreement]] with FISA in March 1981. This agreement stipulated that all teams were obliged to attend all rounds of the championship, while at the same time settling differences over future regulation changes. === Regulation changes and technological development === ==== Sporting regulations ==== The new rules for the 1982 season included an increase in the number of cars permitted to enter a Grand Prix from 30 to 34, and the number of starters from 24 to 26.{{efn|The exemption to this rule was the [[Monaco Grand Prix]], where only 20 cars were allowed to take the start, due to the narrow nature of the track.}} To avoid having all 34 cars on the track at one time, a pre-qualifying session was introduced in which the three teams with the worst record in the previous year would compete to be allowed into qualification proper. Just as the previous year, the best eleven results from all the races counted towards the Drivers' Championship. All races counted towards the Manufacturers Championship.{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=277}} ==== Technology ==== In the years leading up to 1982, two major technological developments had shaped Formula One: the turbocharged engine and "[[Ground effect (cars)|ground effect]]". In {{F1|1977}}, Lotus had revolutionised aerodynamics in Formula One by introducing the [[Lotus 78]], known as the "wing car".{{sfn|Trzesniowski|2010|p=135}} The car used what is commonly referred to as "ground effect", with the physical principle applied being the "[[Venturi effect]]". The sides of the underside of the car would be shut off with skirts to trap the under-pressure airflow underneath the car, effectively "sucking" the vehicle to the ground.{{cite web|title=Re-writing the F1 rule book – Part 1: from wing cars to flat bottoms|url=https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/technical/2017/2/f1-cars-rules-aerodynamics-ground-effect.html|website=formula1.com|publisher=Formula One World Championship Limited|access-date=22 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180122203736/https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/technical/2017/2/f1-cars-rules-aerodynamics-ground-effect.html|archive-date=22 January 2018|date=3 February 2017}} This led to increased cornering speeds, but at the same time brought implications that had an adverse effect on the drivers' safety. Moveable skirts were thus banned in 1981, accompanied by a minimum ride height for the cars of {{convert|6|cm|in|abbr=on}}, targeted at minimising the "ground effect" and to reduce cornering speed.{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=266}} For 1982, both regulations were reversed as a result of the new Concorde Agreement.{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=277}}{{cite journal|last1=Malsher|first1=David|title=A year on the edge|journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]]|date=7 July 2014 |issue=February 2002|page=22|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/february-2002/22/year-edge|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180122203944/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/february-2002/22/year-edge|archive-date=22 January 2018}} The skirts around the underpart of the chassis, which locked the airflow underneath the car, necessitated very stiff suspensions to work properly.{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=277}} This meant that every bump on track was putting enormous strain on the drivers, shaking them around in the cockpit. Additionally, the cornering speed and the resulting high [[g-force]]s put pressure on both the drivers and the cars' suspensions, making them prone to breaking.{{cite web|last1=Collantine|first1=Keith|title=Banned: Ground effect|url=https://www.f1fanatic.co.uk/2007/06/07/banned-ground-effects/|website=F1Fanatic|access-date=22 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180122205553/https://www.f1fanatic.co.uk/2007/06/07/banned-ground-effects/|archive-date=22 January 2018|date=7 June 2007}} The cars would also move up and down on the road, in an effect called "[[ground effect (cars)#Porpoising|porpoising]]", making the cars very hard to control. These adverse effects were particularly impactful at bumpy circuits, such as [[Autódromo Internacional Nelson Piquet|Jacarepaguá]], where Riccardo Patrese retired due to exhaustion. Other drivers reported dizziness and blurred vision.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=49 & 51}} [[File:Keke Rosberg 1982 British GP.jpg|thumb|The [[Cosworth DFV]]-powered [[Williams FW08]] was the last naturally aspirated car used to win the Drivers' Championship until {{F1|1989}}. Pictured here is eventual World Champion [[Keke Rosberg]] at the [[1982 British Grand Prix|British Grand Prix]].|alt=Sideview of a white Williams racing car going through a corner during a race]] The potentially dangerous implications of "ground effect" were only worsened by the advent of very powerful turbocharged engines. In 1977, Renault had introduced the first turbocharged engine into the sport with their [[Renault RS01]]. The regulations at the time allowed for either three-litre normally aspirated or 1.5-litre turbocharged engines, with Renault being the first to attempt to go the latter route.{{cite web|last1=Collantine|first1=Keith|title=Renault RS01: F1's turbo pioneer|url=https://www.f1fanatic.co.uk/2011/07/02/renault-rs01-f1s-turbo-pioneer/|website=F1Fanatic|access-date=22 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180122201337/https://www.f1fanatic.co.uk/2011/07/02/renault-rs01-f1s-turbo-pioneer/|archive-date=22 January 2018|date=2 July 2011}} Over the next few seasons, the turbo engines proved fast, yet unreliable. The cars also suffered from an effect often labelled "turbo lag", meaning that a significant and indeterminable time gap existed between applying the throttle of the car and the point when the full power of the turbo was taking effect. This made the turbo cars very difficult to drive. In {{F1|1979}}, Renault took the first victory with a turbo-charged engine. In 1981, Ferrari had followed them by introducing their own turbo engine. Additionally, the Toleman team also used turbo engines for 1982, supplied by [[Hart Racing Engines|Hart]], while Brabham started using turbocharged BMW engines at some, but not all, rounds that year.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=16–17}} Alfa Romeo retained what motorsport writer [[Doug Nye]] called the most powerful three-litre engine seen in Formula One at that time, with {{convert|548|bhp|kW|abbr=on}}.{{sfn|Nye|1986|p=147}} They tested their turbocharged [[V8]] engine during practice for the [[1982 Italian Grand Prix|Italian Grand Prix]], but did not race with it until {{F1|1983}}.{{cite journal|first=Denis|last=Jenkinson|author-link=Denis Jenkinson|title=The Italian Grand Prix|journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]]|date=7 July 2014 |issue=October 1982|page=46|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/october-1982/46/italian-grand-prix|access-date=21 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180121154006/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/october-1982/46/italian-grand-prix|archive-date=21 January 2018}} Most FOCA teams still relied upon the Cosworth DFV engine, which had been introduced by Lotus in {{F1|1967}}.{{cite web|title=Ford-Cosworth DFV: Eine Ikone der Formel-1-Motoren wird 50|url=http://www.motorsport-total.com/oldtimer/news/ford-cosworth-dfv-eine-ikone-der-formel-1-motoren-wird-50-17032701|website=motorsport-total.com|access-date=22 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180122202537/http://www.motorsport-total.com/oldtimer/news/ford-cosworth-dfv-eine-ikone-der-formel-1-motoren-wird-50-17032701|archive-date=22 January 2018|language=de|date=27 March 2017}} In 1981, McLaren had built the first [[monocoque]] car from [[carbon fibre]] composite. This resulted in lighter cars, while at the same time being more rigid. McLaren had proven that carbon-fibre cars could be quick, with John Watson winning the [[1981 British Grand Prix]]. Watson's lack of severe injuries following a severe accident at [[1981 Italian Grand Prix|that year's Italian Grand Prix]] had shown the superiority of the material in terms of safety.{{cite web|title=Case study: Carbon Fibre|date=2 September 2014 |url=https://www.mclaren.com/technologygroup/case-studies/case-study-carbon-fibre/|publisher=[[McLaren]]|access-date=22 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180122211215/https://www.mclaren.com/technologygroup/case-studies/case-study-carbon-fibre/|archive-date=22 January 2018}} Lotus followed suit for 1982, introducing carbon fibre for their [[Lotus 91]].{{sfn|Pritchard|2015|p=115}} Even with these effective technical advances in chassis design, the FOCA teams with a Cosworth DFV motor had a significant power disadvantage compared to the constructors who used a turbocharged engine. To counteract this, the non-turbo teams used a loophole in the regulations. The weight of the car was measured before and after the race, with oil and cooling liquids allowed to be refilled before the final weigh-in. The teams would therefore build their cars lighter than allowed by the regulations and added water tanks, which they claimed were used to cool brake temperatures, but in reality the water was dumped on the track as soon as the car left the pitlane, allowing them to run faster. Keke Rosberg later explained that "the water tank [...] was the one that gave us at least a theoretical chance to compete with the turbos."{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=52–54}} In other regulation changes, the minimum weight of the cars was reduced from {{convert|585|kg|lb|abbr=on}} to {{convert|580|kg|lb|abbr=on}}. A new "driver survival cell" cockpit protection was made mandatory as well.{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=277}} Four companies, [[Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company|Goodyear]], [[Michelin]], [[Pirelli]], and [[Cooper Tire & Rubber Company|Avon]], supplied tyres, including special qualifying tyres with an increased grip level. These qualifying tyres had originally been banned in {{F1|1980}}, but had since been reallowed.{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=277}} For the first time the number of tyres permitted for qualification was limited to two sets per session,{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=277}} creating a situation which Villeneuve thought "...unnecessarily dangerous. If I have only two chances to set a time, I need a clear track, OK? If it isn't clear, if there's someone in my way, I just have to hope he's looking in his mirrors – I mean, I can't lift, because this is my last chance."{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|pages=175–176}} The necessity of having a clear track to make the most of the short-lasting qualifying tyres led to drivers taking risks, further increasing the danger.{{sfn|Smith|2013|p=277}} == Season report == === Pre-season === The week before the first Grand Prix weekend of the season in South Africa, teams gathered for a test session which was conducted at the Kyalami circuit. Prost set the fastest time during testing, at 1:05.71, almost eight seconds quicker than the previous track record. Surer, driving for the Arrows team, broke his feet in an accident and had to be replaced by Tambay.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=29}} Mass also crashed in his March 821, but escaped uninjured. Ferrari did not have their new car, the [[Ferrari 126C|126C2]], ready for testing and ran an updated version of their 1981 vehicle, the 126CK, instead. The Brabham team were satisfied with the progress of their new [[Brabham BT50|BT50]] with the turbocharged BMW engine. === Championship === ==== Opening rounds ==== {{Multiple image | total_width = 240 | image1 = Didier Pironi 1982.jpg | alt1= Portrait of Didier Pironi | image2 = Lauda at 1982 Dutch Grand Prix.jpg | alt2=Portrait of Niki Lauda | footer = [[Didier Pironi]] ''(left)'' and [[Niki Lauda]] ''(right, both pictured at the [[1982 Dutch Grand Prix]])'' led a drivers' strike at the first race of the season. }} Before the start of the season, all drivers had received a letter from FISA, containing an application form for a new [[FIA Super Licence|Super Licence]]. This new document stated that drivers would not be allowed to switch teams freely during the course of the season, with their licence being withdrawn should they do so. Additionally, the document forbade drivers from actions "which might harm the moral or material interests" of Formula One.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=27}} The returning Lauda was displeased by this and communicated with Pironi, head of the [[Grand Prix Drivers' Association]] (GPDA). They contacted other drivers and ultimately, six drivers refused to sign the document, those being Lauda, Pironi, Villeneuve, Arnoux, [[Bruno Giacomelli]] and [[Andrea de Cesaris]].{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=24–28}} [[File:1982 South African Grand Prix, mechanics in main straight.jpg|thumb|Mechanics play [[association football|football]] on the main straight of [[Kyalami]] during the drivers' strike|alt=Black-and-white photograph of men playing football on a racetrack]] On the Wednesday between testing and the first practice session of the South African Grand Prix, during a meeting of the Formula One Commission,{{efn|The Formula One Commission is a group which discusses and votes upon changes to the sporting regulations of the sport. It consists of the teams, the FIA, race promoters and sponsor representatives.{{cite news |last1=Baldwin |first1=Alan |title=Formula One and FIA present 2021 rules package to teams |url=https://de.reuters.com/article/us-motor-f1-rules/formula-one-and-fia-present-2021-rules-package-to-teams-idUSKCN1R72TU |access-date=15 September 2020 |work=[[Reuters]] |date=26 March 2019 |location=London|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019101701/https://de.reuters.com/article/us-motor-f1-rules/formula-one-and-fia-present-2021-rules-package-to-teams-idUSKCN1R72TU|archive-date=19 October 2020}}}} Pironi, on behalf of the drivers, objected to the licence application. Balestre reacted strongly, excluding all drivers who had not signed from the following day's practice session. The drivers, almost all of them{{efn|[[Jochen Mass]] did not partake in the strike and [[Teo Fabi]] left it midway due to pressure from his team.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=31 & 37}}}} and not just the ones who had refused to sign, in turn reacted by going on strike the next day, boarding a bus to a nearby hotel. The conflict continued until the next day, the Friday before the race was set to take place. It was partially resolved shortly before noon that day, with the drivers receiving half-hearted assurances towards their demands. They would ultimately be fined $5,000 each for the strike, with the new Super Licence being scrapped.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=30–38 & 46}}{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|pages=173–175}} Following the events in South Africa, the GPDA disbanded at a driver meeting in Paris, being replaced by the Professional Racing Drivers' Association (PRDA). When qualifying finally commenced, Arnoux took [[pole position]] from Piquet, with Villeneuve and Patrese on the second row of the grid. At the start, Arnoux led while Piquet did not get away well and was overtaken by several cars, including Prost, who jumped from fifth to second. Piquet and Villeneuve retired early, while Prost took the lead from his teammate Arnoux on lap 14. He would lead until lap 41, when he punctured his left rear tyre, forcing him to come into the pitlane for new tyres. He emerged in eighth place, one lap behind the leader, but with this fresh set, Prost was the quickest driver on the course, allowing him to overtake relatively easily. On lap 68, he once again took the lead from Arnoux and went on to win the race. Reutemann also overtook Arnoux late in the race and finished second, with Lauda in fourth place on his return to Formula One racing.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=39–43}}{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=82–84}}{{cite journal |last1=Jenkinson |first1=Denis |author-link=Denis Jenkinson |title=The South African Grand Prix |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/march-1982/36/south-african-grand-prix |issue=March 1982 |page=36 |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827201126/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/march-1982/36/south-african-grand-prix |archive-date=27 August 2018}} The teams then travelled to Brazil for the second round. Brabham abandoned their turbo-charged BT50 for the time being on grounds of its unreliability, reverting to an updated [[Brabham BT49|BT49D]] for this race, powered by the Cosworth DFV engine.{{sfn|Lang|1992|p=85}} The cars once again proved just how quick they had become, when Prost qualified on pole position 6.27 seconds faster than Piquet had done [[1981 Brazilian Grand Prix|the year before]].{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=175}} Villeneuve was second on the grid and went into the lead at the start, followed by Rosberg, with the two Renault drivers behind. Rosberg fell behind the Renaults on the first lap and was overtaken by Patrese on lap three and by Piquet two laps later. Villeneuve led until lap 30, when he spun out. This allowed Piquet into the lead, closely followed by Rosberg, with the two having battled for position during the preceding laps. The order remained to the finish, with Piquet winning from Rosberg, Prost, Watson and Mansell.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=50–52}}{{cite journal|last=Henry|first=Alan|title=Brazilian Grand Prix|issue=April 1982|page=70|journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]]|date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/april-1982/70/brazilian-grand-prix|access-date=27 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827201631/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/april-1982/70/brazilian-grand-prix|archive-date=27 August 2018}} The heavy strain posed onto the drivers by the bumpy circuit and hot, humid weather was showcased not only by Patrese retiring on lap 34 due to exhaustion, but also when Piquet fainted on the winners' rostrum.{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=84–88}} Following the race, both Ferrari and Renault protested the first- and second-place finishes of Piquet and Rosberg, citing the water tanks used by Brabham and Williams to be illegal. The case was taken to FISA in Paris, with no outcome until after the next race.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=52}} [[File:1982 Alfa Romeo 182.jpg|thumb|[[Andrea de Cesaris]] (''left'') took a surprise [[pole position]] at [[1982 United States Grand Prix West|Long Beach]] in his [[Alfa Romeo 182]] (''pictured'').|alt=Two men in suits standing left and right of a red-and-white racing car]] The third race of the season took place at the [[street circuit]] in [[Long Beach]]. During Saturday's qualifying, Lauda did just one run of a few laps, setting a fast time that put him on top of the leaderboard. In the closing seconds of the session, de Cesaris bettered Lauda's time, clinching pole position for Alfa Romeo. De Cesaris had been ousted by McLaren for Lauda over the winter and was moved to tears by his accomplishment.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=61–66}} De Cesaris led from the start, while Lauda was overtaken by Arnoux for second place. On lap six, Giacomelli, running fourth, tried to outbrake Lauda and in the process hit Arnoux, forcing both to retire. This allowed Villeneuve into third place, ahead of Watson. Pironi and Prost both retired after hitting the wall on laps seven and eleven respectively. On lap 15, Lauda took advantage of de Cesaris missing a gear change and moved into the lead, immediately beginning to pull away. Rosberg overtook Villeneuve for third on lap 21. This turned into second place on lap 34, when de Cesaris crashed into the wall after his engine had failed. The order remained until the [[chequered flag]], with Lauda winning in only his third Grand Prix back in the sport.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=61–66}}{{cite journal |last1=Jenkinson |first1=Denis |author-link=Denis Jenkinson |title=United States (West) Grand Prix |issue=May 1982 |page=46 |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/may-1982/46/united-stateswest-grand-prix |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827202004/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/may-1982/46/united-stateswest-grand-prix |archive-date=27 August 2018}} Villeneuve was later excluded from the results in Long Beach, following a protest by [[Ken Tyrrell]] over Ferrari's use of a double rear wing.{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=88–92}} ==== First European rounds ==== In the week before the next round, the [[1982 San Marino Grand Prix|San Marino Grand Prix]], the FIA International Court of Appeal sided with Ferrari and Renault on their complaint over the water tanks at the race in Brazil and disqualified Piquet and Rosberg, handing victory to Prost. It was further decided that the cars would now be weighed after the race in the condition in which they had finished, eliminating the Cosworth-powered teams' use of water tanks to increase their performance.{{sfn|Lang|1992|p=92}} All other runners' results from the Brazilian Grand Prix were upheld, including Watson's, who inherited second place even though his use of the water tanks had been as illegal as the others.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=71}}{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|pages=178–180}} The FOCA teams requested a postponement of the next race until July to allow consideration of the effects of the court's judgement, on the grounds that it changed the regulations of the sport. The race organisers refused to delay the race, which went ahead without the majority of the FOCA teams.{{sfn|Lang|1992|p=92}} At this stage in the championship, Prost led with 18 points, six ahead of Lauda, with Rosberg and Watson sharing third position on eight points.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=67}} With the FOCA teams boycotting the race, the San Marino Grand Prix was run with just 14 cars present.{{efn|The [[Tyrrell Racing|Tyrrell]] team, although a member of FOCA, attended the event. They were exempted from the boycott due to Italian sponsors providing much-needed money for the team.{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=180}}}} The turbocharged Renaults and Ferraris were heavily favoured and Arnoux duly took pole position ahead of Prost, with Villeneuve and Pironi on the second row. Due to the fast nature of the [[Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari|Imola track]], Ferrari team boss [[Mauro Forghieri]] told his drivers to save fuel. Arnoux led from the start while Prost lost two positions to the Ferrari drivers on the first lap. He eventually retired on lap seven. After some changes of position with Villeneuve and Pironi, Arnoux pulled away, but retired as well after 44 laps when his engine expired. This left only the Ferrari drivers in a position to win the Grand Prix. Their team held out "slow" signs from the pit wall, urging them to conserve fuel. Villeneuve, who led, understood this to mean that the cars were to finish in the current order. Pironi appeared to disregard the signals from the pitwall and took the lead on lap 46. He then sped up, pulling Villeneuve with him, who retook the lead again on lap 49. They changed position three more times; as Villeneuve slowed down each time he took the lead, Pironi would overtake him again. Eventually, Pironi won the race and Villeneuve was furious at his teammate for allegedly not following team orders.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=68–79}}{{cite journal|last1=Jenkinson|first1=Denis|author-link=Denis Jenkinson|title=The San Marino Grand Prix|issue=June 1982|page=104|journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]]|date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/june-1982/104/san-marino-grand-prix|access-date=27 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827202154/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/june-1982/104/san-marino-grand-prix|archive-date=27 August 2018}} After the race, he said: "People seem to think we had the battle of our lives! [...] I was coasting those last 15 laps." Pironi said that "The 'slow' sign means only to use your head [... not that] if you think you can win, don't do it." In an interview the following week, Villeneuve said that he would never speak to Pironi again.{{sfn|Donaldson|2003|pages=289–290}} {{quote box|quote="I've declared war. Absolute war. Finishing second is one thing – I'd have been mad at myself for not being quick enough if he'd beaten me. But finishing second because the bastard steals it..."
[[Gilles Villeneuve]] describing his relationship with teammate [[Didier Pironi]] after the [[1982 San Marino Grand Prix|San Marino Grand Prix]].{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|pages=183}}|width=31%|align=right}} Two weeks later, the paddock moved to [[Circuit Zolder|Zolder]] for the Belgian Grand Prix. In qualifying, Villeneuve went out onto the track on his second set of fast tyres, which were already used and had only one more fast lap to go before their performance became compromised. On his flying lap, he failed to better the time of teammate Pironi, but instead of slowing down, as drivers usually did on laps at the end of which they were supposed to head back to the pits, Villeneuve continued to drive fast.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=85–87}} It has been speculated that he was determined to beat Pironi's time due to the animosity between the two.{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=96–97}}{{sfn|Watkins|1997|p=98}} It is unclear if this is true, with Forghieri claiming that Villeneuve had indeed planned to return to the pitlane.{{sfn|Donaldson|2003|pages=296–298}} In any event, Villeneuve caught Jochen Mass travelling much more slowly through a left-handed bend and moved to the right to pass him at the same instant that Mass also moved right to let Villeneuve through on the [[racing line]]. The two collided and Villeneuve was thrown out of his disintegrating car. He died of a [[cervical fracture|fractured neck]] in a local hospital at 9:12 that evening.{{sfn|Donaldson|2003|pages=296–298}} Ferrari withdrew from the race, which Watson won for McLaren.{{cite journal |title=Belgian Grand Prix |issue=June 1982 |page=88 |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/june-1982/88/belgian-grand-prix |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827202434/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/june-1982/88/belgian-grand-prix |archive-date=27 August 2018}} His teammate Lauda, who had finished third behind Rosberg, was disqualified after the race for an underweight car. The results were dominated by the returning FOCA teams; even the only turbo-engined finisher, Piquet, was one of them, after Brabham reintroduced the BMW-powered BT50 for this race.{{cite journal |last1=Jenkinson |first1=Denis |title=Notes on the cars at Zolder |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |issue=June 1982 |page=49 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/june-1982/49/notes-on-the-cars-at-zolder-3 |access-date=27 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019102052/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/june-1982/49/notes-on-the-cars-at-zolder-3|archive-date=19 October 2020}}{{sfn|Bamsey|1983|p=51}} Motorsport journalist [[Nigel Roebuck]] stated that the next race, the [[1982 Monaco Grand Prix|Monaco Grand Prix]], "was a sombre, edgy place [...] the sense of [Villeneuve's] absence was overwhelming"; the Canadian had lived in the principality and had won [[1981 Monaco Grand Prix|the previous year's race]].{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=186}} Ferrari chose to only run one car, not replacing Villeneuve for the time being.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=117}} In the race itself, Arnoux led early on from pole position before spinning off, handing the lead to his Renault teammate Prost. The latter in turn built up a massive lead, but a light rain shower in the closing laps triggered a chaotic finish. Prost crashed out, handing the lead to Patrese, still running the Cosworth-powered Brabham BT49D.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=108}} Patrese spun on the penultimate lap and stalled, allowing Pironi into the lead, followed by de Cesaris. On the final lap, Pironi, de Cesaris, and Daly all retired because they ran out of fuel while in potential race winning positions. Meanwhile, Patrese bump-started his car by coasting down a hill, completed the final two laps, and took his first career victory.{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=187}}{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=99–102}} Pironi was classified second, despite running out of fuel and stopping on the last lap.{{cite journal |last1=Jenkinson |first1=Denis |author-link=Denis Jenkinson |title=The Monaco Grand Prix |issue=July 1982 |page=62 |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1982/62/monaco-grand-prix |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827202633/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1982/62/monaco-grand-prix |archive-date=27 August 2018}} After the race, Prost, who had scored no points since the Brazilian Grand Prix in March, led the championship by one point from Watson and two points from Pironi.{{sfn|Bamsey|1983|p=57}} ==== North American rounds ==== [[File:Nelson Piquet 1982 British GP.jpg|thumb|Defending champion [[Nelson Piquet]] ''(pictured at the [[1982 British Grand Prix|British Grand Prix]])'', failed to qualify in [[1982 Detroit Grand Prix|Detroit]], but won the [[1982 Canadian Grand Prix|next race in Canada]].|alt=Sideview of a white-and-dark blue Brabham racing car during a race]] The next race was the inaugural [[1982 Detroit Grand Prix|Detroit Grand Prix]], which was marred by lack of track preparation, delaying the practice session on a circuit that had never hosted a motor race before. During the shortened qualifying session, Prost took pole position ahead of de Cesaris, with Rosberg in third. The big surprise of the day was defending World Champion Piquet, who failed to qualify as his Brabham BT50 had engine problems and the spare car was not performing well either. In the race, Prost led comfortably until an accident between [[Roberto Guerrero]], [[Elio de Angelis]] and Patrese led to the race being suspended. De Cesaris had retired at this point and at the restart, Prost led Rosberg and Pironi. A problem with the fuel injection slowed Prost down, handing the lead to Rosberg. Watson, who qualified 17th on the grid, got his Michelin tyres working well on the Detroit circuit and overtook one driver after another until, on lap 37, he went into the lead, as Rosberg had gearbox issues. Watson won the race from [[Eddie Cheever]] and Pironi, taking the lead in the World Championship.{{cite journal|first=Denis|last=Jenkinson|author-link=Denis Jenkinson|title=The Grand Prix of Detroit|journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]]|issue=July 1982|pages=43–47|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1982/43/grand-prix-detroit|access-date=6 March 2018|archive-date=6 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180306101113/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1982/43/grand-prix-detroit|url-status=dead}}{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=103–107}} Tragedy struck again at the [[1982 Canadian Grand Prix|Canadian Grand Prix]]. Pironi qualified on pole, but stalled at the start. His stationary car was hit by the Osella of young Italian Riccardo Paletti, who was competing in only his second race in Formula One. Paletti suffered severe internal injuries and his car caught fire while the track marshals tried to extract him from his vehicle. He was pronounced dead upon arrival in the hospital. The race was restarted and won by Piquet in the BMW-powered Brabham ahead of teammate Patrese, still in the Cosworth-powered BT49D. It would be the last one-two finish for the Brabham team in their Formula One history.{{cite journal |last1=Frankel |first1=Andrew |title=Simply the Best |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |issue=May 1999 |pages=46–49 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/may-1999/46/simply-the-best |access-date=9 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019102205/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/may-1999/46/simply-the-best|archive-date=19 October 2020}} Watson finished third to consolidate his lead in the championship.{{cite journal|first=Denis|last=Jenkinson|author-link=Denis Jenkinson|title=The Canadian Grand Prix|journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]]|issue=July 1982|pages=48–50|url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1982/48/canadian-grand-prix|access-date=6 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180306104905/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/july-1982/48/canadian-grand-prix|archive-date=6 March 2018|url-status=dead}} After the Canadian round, Watson was on 30 points, ten ahead of Pironi, followed by Patrese on 19, Prost with 18 and Rosberg with 17 points.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=151}} ==== Back to Europe ==== At the [[1982 Dutch Grand Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]], Ferrari introduced Patrick Tambay as a replacement for Villeneuve. The Renault drivers once more locked out the front row, Arnoux ahead of Prost. The latter took the lead at the start, followed by Arnoux and Pironi. On lap two, Pironi overtook Arnoux and three laps later moved ahead of Prost into the lead. While Prost retired with an engine failure, Arnoux was lucky to survive a heavy accident on lap 22 at Tarzan corner. His left front wheel broke off as he approached the corner, sending his car into the tyre wall. Pironi won the race without serious competition, ahead of Piquet and Rosberg.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=160–173}}{{cite web |title=Dutch GP, 1982 |url=http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr366.html |website=grandprix.com |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827204001/http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr366.html |archive-date=27 August 2018}} [[File:Niki Lauda 1982 British GP.jpg|thumb|[[Niki Lauda]] won two races in his comeback season, first in [[1982 United States Grand Prix West|Long Beach]], then in the [[1982 British Grand Prix|United Kingdom]] ''(pictured)''.|alt=Sideview of a red-and-white McLaren racing car during a race]] For the next race at Brands Hatch, the [[1982 British Grand Prix|British Grand Prix]], Brabham had devised what they referred to as "The Ploy". Inspired by Prost's comeback drive at the season opener at Kyalami, the team planned to send out their cars with tanks only half full and softer, and therefore faster, tyres. A pit stop midway through the race was supposed to refuel the car and change tyres, giving the Brabham drivers the advantage to be able to lap quicker than everybody else and gain enough of a lead to win.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=174–178}} On top of that, both drivers were now committed to the BMW-powered BT50 chassis.{{cite journal |last1=Jenkinson |first1=Denis |title=The British Grand Prix: Summer Fayre |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=5 May 2015 |issue=August 1982 |page=1014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/issues/august-1982 |access-date=9 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019102329/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/issues/august-1982|archive-date=19 October 2020}} In qualifying, Rosberg surprised by taking only the second, and last, non-turbocharged pole position of the season. At the start of the warm-up lap, a fuel pressure issue led to his car being stationary on the grid while the other cars got underway. His mechanics helped him to a push start, but he did not reach the field in time and had to start the race last. This handed the front starting spot to Patrese, but he stalled. Both Arnoux and Fabi ran into him, taking all three out on the spot. Piquet as the only remaining Brabham left led from Lauda, but "The Ploy" was not to be executed, as Piquet retired with fuel injection problems on lap ten. This left Lauda to take his second victory of the season, followed by Pironi and Tambay. Pironi took over the lead of the championship, now five points ahead of Watson.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=182–189}}{{cite web |title=British GP, 1982 |url=http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr367.html |website=grandprix.com |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827204110/http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr367.html |archive-date=27 August 2018}} {{multiple image | direction = vertical | width = 240px | image1 = Pironi and Alboreto at 1982 Dutch Grand Prix.jpg | alt1=Black-and-white photograph of two racing cars going through a corner | image2 = Grand Prix op Zandvoort wagen Arnoux in de vangrail, Bestanddeelnr 253-8756.jpg | alt2=A badly damaged yellow-and-white racing car after impact into a tyre wall | footer = [[Didier Pironi]] ''(top)'' won the [[1982 Dutch Grand Prix|Dutch Grand Prix]] for [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]], while [[René Arnoux]] survived a heavy accident ''(bottom)''.}} The Renaults were dominant at their home race, the French Grand Prix at [[Circuit Paul Ricard]]. Arnoux qualified ahead of Prost, and with Prost being better positioned in the championship, the team decided that if the cars should run first and second, he should win. Arnoux did not honour the agreement and took the victory ahead of his teammate, much to Prost's dismay. Another heavy accident marred the race, as Mass ran into the back of [[Mauro Baldi]] at Signes corner. As Mass's car slid towards the barrier, it was catapulted into the grandstands full of spectators. Although several people had minor injures, the accident did not result in any fatalities or serious injuries.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=194–201}}{{sfn|Lang|1992|pages=119–122}}{{cite journal |last1=Jenkinson |first1=Denis |author-link=Denis Jenkinson |title=The French Grand Prix |issue=September 1982 |page=107 |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/september-1982/107/french-grand-prix |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827204156/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/september-1982/107/french-grand-prix |archive-date=27 August 2018}} At this stage, Pironi led the championship by nine points ahead of Watson{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=201}} and was seen as the likely favourite to win the title. At the following event, the German Grand Prix at [[Hockenheimring|Hockenheim]], Pironi qualified on pole position, but collided with Prost's Renault in wet conditions later in the session. Pironi's car was thrown into the air and though he survived the impact, he suffered severe leg injuries and would never compete in Formula One again.{{sfn|Lang|1992|p=123}} The race took place with the first slot on the grid vacant.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=206}} Brabham were again attempting to employ the strategy of having their cars refuel and change tyres halfway through the race. Piquet led comfortably when he collided with Salazar while trying to lap him, leading Piquet to furiously hit and kick his competitor after he got out of the car. Tambay went on to win the race for Ferrari, his first victory in a Grand Prix, ahead of Arnoux and Rosberg, who was now third in the championship.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=211–215}}{{cite journal |last1=Jenkinson |first1=Denis |author-link=Denis Jenkinson |title=The German Grand Prix |issue=September 1982 |page=41 |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/september-1982/41/german-grand-prix |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827204359/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/september-1982/41/german-grand-prix |archive-date=27 August 2018}} At the [[1982 Austrian Grand Prix|Austrian Grand Prix]] on the [[Österreichring]], most turbocharged runners retired early, leaving Prost in the lead, only to retire with fuel injection issues five laps from the finish.{{sfn|Lang|1992|p=129}} This left de Angelis and Rosberg to fight out the race victory, with de Angelis reaching the finish line 0.050 seconds ahead to win his first ever Grand Prix.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|p=227}}{{cite web |title=Austrian GP, 1982 |url=http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr370.html |website=grandprix.com |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827204552/http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr370.html |archive-date=27 August 2018}} The Grand Prix also saw the Brabham drivers make it to their mid-race pit stops for the first time, only for both to retire later on.{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|pages=211–212}} Rosberg in turn achieved his maiden victory at the next race, the [[1982 Swiss Grand Prix|Swiss Grand Prix]], held at the Dijon-Prenois circuit and scheduled for 80 laps. By now, several other teams planned and executed fuel-and-tyres pit stops, with varying degrees of success. The Renaults of Prost and Arnoux had qualified on the front row. Rosberg, consistently lapping quicker than all other drivers, was held up by de Cesaris, but eventually found a way past him. He overtook Arnoux on lap 73 and Prost on lap 78 to take the lead and the race victory. In doing so, he also took the lead in the championship.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=238–241}}{{cite journal |title=The Swiss Grand Prix |issue=October 1982 |page=42 |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=7 July 2014 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/october-1982/42/swiss-grand-prix |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827204648/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/october-1982/42/swiss-grand-prix |archive-date=27 August 2018}} At the Italian Grand Prix, Mario Andretti returned to take over the seat at Ferrari left vacant by Pironi and qualified in pole position. The race was won by Arnoux, leading home the Ferraris of Tambay and Andretti. Rosberg did not score points, having finished eighth. Watson meanwhile took three points for fourth place, leaving him with a mathematical chance of winning the title; this would require him to win the last race of the season with Rosberg failing to score.{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=246–257}} ==== Last round and title decision ==== {{quote box|quote="To be honest, I've hated every second of this season. There's something very wrong when the [[chequered flag]] comes down, and all you feel is relief that another race weekend is out of the way without someone getting killed."
[[Fédération Internationale du Sport Automobile|FISA]] circuit inspector Derek Ongaro speaking about the 1982 season.{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=217}}|width=25%|align=right}} At the last race of the season, the [[1982 Caesars Palace Grand Prix|Caesars Palace Grand Prix]] in [[Las Vegas]], Prost took pole position ahead of Arnoux. The race was held in {{convert|98.8|F|C|order=flip}} degree weather during a particularly hot time of year in Las Vegas. While Arnoux retired from the race itself, Prost was hampered by blistering tyres to finish fourth. [[Michele Alboreto]] took a surprising victory for Tyrrell. Watson finished second, meaning that Rosberg's fifth-place finish was enough to secure the title.{{cite web |title=United States GP, 1982 |url=http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr373.html |website=grandprix.com |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180827205139/http://www.grandprix.com/gpe/rr373.html |archive-date=27 August 2018}}{{sfn|Hilton|2007|pages=264–273}}{{cite journal |title=1982 Las Vegas Grand Prix race report |journal=[[Motor Sport (magazine)|Motor Sport]] |date=November 1982 |pages=43–46 |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/november-1982/43/las-vegas-grand-prix |access-date=28 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019102515/https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/november-1982/43/las-vegas-grand-prix|archive-date=19 October 2020}} He became the first driver since [[Mike Hawthorn]] in {{F1|1958}} to clinch the championship having won just one Grand Prix.{{cite web|title=Elegant champion: Hawthorn triumphs in F1 with style|url=http://70.ferrari.com/en/legacy/story/elegant-champion|website=ferrari.com|publisher=[[Scuderia Ferrari]]|access-date=7 March 2018}} === Post-season === The 1982 season was the last for Lotus team owner [[Colin Chapman]], who died on 16 December 1982 having suffered a heart attack.{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=217}} Following "a season touched by tragedy, clouded in controversy and enveloped in excitement", FISA announced that the "ground effect" would be banned for {{F1|1983}} to make the cars safer.{{sfn|Roebuck|1999|p=217}} Overall, the 1982 season saw 11 different winners in 16 races, with no driver scoring more than two victories. The 1982 FIA Formula One World Championship was the 36th season of FIA Formula One motor racing. It included two competitions run over the course of the year, the 33rd Formula One World Championship for Drivers and the 25th Formula One World Championship for Constructors. The season featured sixteen rounds between 23 January and 25 September. The Drivers' Championship was won by Keke Rosberg and the Constructors' Championship by Scuderia Ferrari.

The Championship started with a drivers' strike at the season opener in South Africa and saw a partial race boycott as part of the ongoing FISA–FOCA war at the San Marino Grand Prix. Two drivers died during 1982: Gilles Villeneuve during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix and Riccardo Paletti at the start of the Canadian Grand Prix. Championship front-runner Didier Pironi also suffered a career-ending accident while qualifying for the German Grand Prix. These incidents and several other major accidents led to regulation changes to increase driver safety for the 1983 season. Motorsport journalist Nigel Roebuck later wrote that 1982 was "an ugly year, pock-marked by tragedy, by dissension, by greed, and yet, paradoxically, it produced some of the most memorable racing ever seen".[1]

Eventual champion Rosberg won only one race all season – the Swiss Grand Prix – but consistency gave him the Drivers' Championship, five points clear of Pironi and John Watson. Rosberg was the second driver to win the championship having won only one race in the season, after Mike Hawthorn in 1958. Eleven different drivers from seven different teams won a race during the season, with no driver winning more than twice; there was also a run of nine different winners in nine consecutive races from the Monaco Grand Prix to the Swiss Grand Prix. Ferrari, who replaced Villeneuve with Patrick Tambay and Pironi with 1978 World Champion Mario Andretti, managed to score enough points to secure the Constructors' Championship, finishing five points clear of McLaren with Renault third. Rosberg's team Williams finished fourth in the Constructors' standing a further four points behind McLaren, marking the only time since the Constructors' Championship was introduced in 1958 that a team containing the eventual Drivers' Champion finished outside the top 3 of the Constructors' standings.

Team changes

[edit]

All teams and constructors who had competed in 1981 returned for the new season. Brabham had entered an engine supply deal with German car manufacturer BMW for the use of their inline-four turbo engines. The team announced in January that they were committing to the use of the new BMW engine throughout the season,[3] but after experiencing reliability problems with it, they reverted to the Cosworth DFV motor several times during the season.[4]

Driver changes

[edit]

At the end of the 1981 season, both Williams drivers, 1980 World Champion Alan Jones and Carlos Reutemann, had announced their retirement from racing.[5] Reutemann did in fact return for 1982,[6] competing in the first two races, before retiring unexpectedly at the end of March.[7] Jones was replaced by Keke Rosberg, who had previously entered 36 Grands Prix, with a third-place finish as his best result.[8]

The off season saw rumours of several former champions returning to the sport,[a] but in the end only double World Champion Niki Lauda returned to Formula One after an absence of two years to partner John Watson at McLaren.[9] Ferrari and Renault retained their race-winning line-ups of Gilles Villeneuve and Didier Pironi and Alain Prost and René Arnoux, respectively.[10] At Brabham, defending World Champion Nelson Piquet remained with the team, and was partnered by Riccardo Patrese, who moved from Arrows to replace Héctor Rebaque.[5]

The Osella team gave Riccardo Paletti his Grand Prix debut, while Toleman replaced Brian Henton with Teo Fabi, also a newcomer to Formula One.[11] Marc Surer was hired by Arrows, but broke both his feet in pre-season testing at Kyalami. He was set to be replaced by Patrick Tambay, who was then fired after taking part in the drivers' strike at that race and the seat went to Henton.[12] Eliseo Salazar transferred from Ensign Racing to the ATS team.[13]

Mid-season changes

Following Reutemann's retirement, Williams hired 1978 World Champion Mario Andretti as a one-off replacement for the United States Grand Prix West.[7] Derek Daly then became the permanent second driver at the team, as Andretti had racing obligations in the United States to fulfill.[14] Andretti returned with Ferrari for the last two races of the season, replacing Pironi, who had suffered career-ending injuries at the German Grand Prix.[15] Villeneuve, who died following a crash in qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix, was replaced by Tambay starting from the Dutch Grand Prix.[16]

At Team Lotus, Nigel Mansell missed two races due to injuries from a crash in Canada. His substitute at the Dutch Grand Prix was Roberto Moreno, who failed to qualify.[17] Mansell attempted a comeback at Brands Hatch, but was again replaced at the French Grand Prix, this time by Geoff Lees.[18] An accident at the race in France led Jochen Mass, already deeply shaken by the fatal crash of Villeneuve, in which he was involved, to walk away from Grand Prix racing.[19] He was replaced at March by Rupert Keegan.[20] Swedish driver Slim Borgudd had moved from ATS to Tyrrell in the off season, but was forced to leave the team after only three races when his sponsorship money ran out.[21] Henton took his place from the Belgian Grand Prix onwards, as Surer returned to Arrows after his injuries had healed.[22]
